habitat: Well-wooded rivers and bushes or thickets standing in floodwater. Usually solitary, and largely crepuscular or nocturnal. It may sky-point, and it perches in a tree when flushed.
summary: A tiny bittern with slate-grey upperparts, heavily streaked underparts, and orange-yellow legs and feet that often hang down in flight. The immature is rufous below, with rufous-tipped feathers above. The flight is direct and pigeon-like. Newman calls it an uncommon summer resident and visitor, and nomadic.

similar.note: Little Bittern has black-and-buff wings. A young one is paler below and has olive legs, not the orange-yellow legs and slate-grey back of a Dwarf Bittern.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^6=64 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 32–128.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

wings.pattern: Orange-yellow legs and feet often hang down in flight.

viewNotes.note: Slate-grey above, streaked below, with orange-yellow legs.
Grey face and a streaked throat.
Direct, pigeon-like flight. The upperwing colour is not named separately from the slate-grey upperparts.
Legs often hang down. The underwing colour was not named.

calls.description: Newman does not describe the voice. The texts do not separate the sexes. The catalogue cut is not labelled by sex. Grade A from South Africa, under the older genus Ixobrychus. The filename is a date, not the species name.

research.note: Status is an intra-African migrant. Newman calls it a summer resident and visitor, so the southern summer months, October to March, are listed. It is also nomadic. Chick down is not described. The call is grade A from South Africa.
